biography.name: Avery Larkin

background.family: Lives with their father, his partner, and a younger stepsister.
background.finances: Steady middle income; family budgets carefully for travel.
background.geography: Albuquerque, New Mexico; aunt lives in Lubbock, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English; participates in a neighborhood mutual-aid group with family.
background.school: Public high school with a flexible arts track.
background.accessOpportunities: City museums and public workshops; Texas visits possible through relatives.

timeline.story: In 2014, Avery loved making enormous paper animals and disliked when adults folded them neatly for storage. Their father began photographing each creation, which made letting the temporary structures go a little easier.

At six, they learned basic gardening at a community plot. During 2017, they preferred observing ants to watering seedlings and invented stories about where the insects were trying to go with oversized crumbs.

In 2018, Avery took a pottery class and found the wheel frustrating. Hand building felt better, and they proudly made a lopsided vessel designed to hold exactly the collection of pencils they used at school.

During 2020, Avery began exchanging illustrated postcards with an aunt in Lubbock. They enjoyed the slow response time and researched the landscapes between their homes, though they had little interest in posting their drawings online.

At twelve, they started volunteering at a community fridge with family. In 2023, they helped replace confusing donation signs and discovered they were comfortable correcting adults when the rule protected the food people would receive.

Across 2024 and 2025, Avery experimented with stop-motion animation and grew tomatoes. They liked patient repetitive movements in animation, yet repeatedly forgot plant watering until they set a shared reminder with their stepsister.

At sixteen in 2026, Avery is exploring a Texas summer art workshop near their aunt and a local environmental club. They are unsure whether they want formal creative study or prefer keeping art separate from graded expectations. Their newest film uses kitchen utensils as characters, with their stepsister supplying increasingly improbable dialogue.

motivations: Making ordinary spaces feel cared for
ambitions: They picture an adult life with close neighbors, a small garden, and room for several unfinished projects.
struggles: Worries that grading might flatten enjoyment

biography.selfDescription: I can spend an hour moving a tiny paper foot for a film and still forget to water a real plant. I like making things slowly, especially when somebody else will actually use or see them nearby.

Would they miss community familiarity in a distant setting?
